en: Having bowed to the Veda-Person (Vedapuruṣa), I shall declare the compendium of accents (*svarasaṃgraha*).
The accents (*svara*) are the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the monotone (*pracaya*);
they are seen depending upon the syllables (*akṣara*) within the collections of phonemes (*varṇarāśi*).
The length of the body, the firmness of the limbs,
and the thinness of the space within the ears are the signs for birth in a high family;
whereas the shortness of the body and the softness of the limbs [are signs of low birth].
The greatness of the ear and of space are the causes for birth in a low [register];
the cause for the production of the *svarita* is the combination of these two.
The well-known nature of the *pracaya* (circumflex) is that it is indeed heard as having an acute (*udātta*) quality.
These vowels function especially among the gods:
*udātta* is Agni, *nihata* (anudātta) is Vāyu, and *svarita* is Sūrya.
Those gods proceed in the form of fire (*vahni*) in three ways within the Śruti.
In this very world is Pavamāna Agni, while Pāvaka Agni is in the intermediate space; in that world above, he is called by the wise as Agni-śruti.
He is recited as "the hair-bearing Agni" because his flames, lightning, and rays are his hair.
That fire always dwells in the right hand of the brahmin. Right there, all sacred fords (tīrthas) and all the gods, including Vāsava, reside;
and the Vedas, resting upon his fingers, proceed with their own melodic accents.
And the Supreme Self, residing there within that very thumb, eternally dances; He is the supreme one known as Śabdabrahman among the Vedas.
Therefore, the twice-born who meditates upon the Veda [should do so] with a hand resembling the ear of a cow.

In the head, heart, throat, and root [of the genitals], and in all the mouths, they arise in sequence from the vowels *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *a* as the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes. Likewise,
they are located at the beginning of the index finger (*tarjanī*), the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), and similarly at the middle finger (*anāmikā*) and the last [the ring finger].
One should show [the *pracaya*] by means of the thumb at the middle of the middle finger.
From an *udātta* comes the *nihata*; from a *svarita*, the *pracaya* arises.
(13) From an *udātta*, the *svarita* occurs either before or even after the *nihata*.
A *jātya* [svarita] is an *abhinihita-kṣaipra*, or it may also be a *praśliṣṭa* that lacks its own accent;

it attains the state of being *nihata* (suppressed) when following an acute (*udātta*) vowel, whether immediately after or even further back, and there is no *pracaya* (accumulation/accentuation) beyond it. 14–15.
The *svarita* [accent] follows after the *pracaya*, and after the *nihata* (low-pitched), the *pracaya* follows;
after a *svarita*, there occurs the *pracaya* of the subsequent *anudātta* (unaccented) syllables.
That which has a *udātta* or *svarita* as its penultimate syllable is [treated as such] everywhere, up to the limit of the *nihata*.

In the case of a *parigraha* (enclitic), when low-pitched (*anudātta*) syllables follow, they do not become high-pitched (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) if a following *udātta* or *svarita* syllable exists. (17) In the *parigraha* of *tanūnapāt* and *śacīpati*, the circumflex (*svarita*) quality arises; however, when there is a merging with a preceding low-pitched (*nīca*) tone, it becomes a single unified *svarita*. (18)
A low note attains highness, and a high note attains lowness, by means of three [factors];
likewise, the letters *ya* and *va*, when joined with consonants, [attain their respective qualities].
In that case, the vowel would be either original (*apūrva*) or preceded by a low [consonant] according to its genus (*jāti*). 19.

When the two vowels *i* and *u* become *y* and *v* respectively, one should always know this as the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* [svarita] accent when followed by an unraised (*anudātta*) vowel. Where *e* or *o*, being raised (*udātta*), are followed by a low (*nīca*) vowel *a*, [the same applies]. (20–21)
Where there is a single unified state (*ekībhāva*), the *svara* is called *abhinihita*:
if the vowel *i* precedes and the vowel *a* follows, and the latter is elided (*nihata*).
Teachers who are experts in phonetics call this *praśliṣṭa*. 22.

Where there is a *svarita* immediately following an *avagraha*, one should know that it is *tirovirāma*. If the *avagraha* itself is *udātta*, whatever follows it in the Vedic meters shall be *svarita*. 23–24.

This entire [recitation] is called *bahusvara* and is designated as *tairovyañjana*. Where there is a *svarita* vowel in a hiatus (*vivṛti*), and where it occurs in a conjunction (*saṃyuta*), that should be understood as a *pādavṛtta*; [it is so called] because of the hiatus and because the vowel becomes low-pitched (*nīca*).

The *jātya*, the *abhinihita-svāra*, the *kṣaipra*, and the *praśliṣṭa*—these are the accents that tremble where there is the rise of the acute (*udātta*) or the circumflex (*svarita*). They occur when preceded by an acute in a short vowel; otherwise, they occur when preceded by a grave (*nīca*). 26–27.
One should perform the *krama* when there is an unaccented (*anudātta*) vowel; for one should rely upon the circumflex (*svarita*).
Then, the unaccented (*nihata*) should arrive, followed by the rule for low trembling (*nīcakampa*).
One should begin first with the acute (*udātta*) and conclude with the unaccented (*nihata*).
That should be known as a short tremor (*hrasvakampa*); the illustration is: *kvā vo 'śvāḥ kvā*.
That which is a natural tone (*jātya*) with a natural [pause] is called a *kṣaipra* in the case of Agni;
"they increased" (*te 'vardhanta*) is an *abhinihita*; "O Indra, lover of songs" (*indra girvaṇaḥ*) is a *praśliṣṭa*. 29–30.
In the *viṣkambhita* [intonation], there is the *tairovirāma*; in the *tairovyañjana*, there is the *ūtaye* and the *pādavṛtta*.
Who indeed knows the manifestation of the proximity of the *svara*?
The *svara*, the *varṇa*, the *akṣara*, the *mātrā*, and the purpose of the application (*viniyoga*)—these are the [elements]. 31.
One who desires to understand mantras must know this at every step:
a mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, if incorrectly applied, does not convey its intended meaning;
that thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Vṛtra] was destroyed due to a lapse in accent. 32–33.
He who studies [the Veda] devoid of the proper accents and phonemes,
being consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman verses, goes to a low birth.
But he who studies the Veda with his hand [in the proper manner], endowed with the correct accents, phonemes, and meanings—
Purified by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman [Vedas], he is glorified in the world of Brahman. 35.
Thus ends the training in accents.
